title: Vayakhel: too much (Exodus 36:5–7)
hook: the people bring so much that Moses asks them to stop

segments.voice: Yesterday, kehillah: Moses gathered the people again, this time for something good. Your line was gather the people. Did you send that first message? Day three hundred sixty-nine.

Every fundraiser in history has the same worry: will enough come in? Every school bake sale, every roof appeal, every online campaign with a little bar creeping toward the goal. Now picture the opposite. The money pours in so fast that the people running the project walk into the leader's office and say, please, make them stop. There's too much. That has happened, at least once, and the Torah wrote it down. It happened in the desert, with a camp of former slaves, building a sanctuary out of what they carried.
screen: `WILL ENOUGH COME IN?` → `PLEASE, MAKE THEM STOP.` → `IT HAPPENED IN THE DESERT.`

segments.voice: Moses has asked for gifts for the sanctuary from everyone whose heart moves them: gold, silver, bronze, blue and purple yarn, linen, goat hair, wood, oil, spices, stones. The text says they kept bringing, morning after morning. Then the craftspeople stop their work and come to Moses. The people are bringing much more than enough, they say. So Moses sends word through the whole camp: no man or woman should make anything more for the offering. And the Torah adds, so the people were held back from bringing. Then one last line, in the JPS 1917 translation: "For the stuff they had was sufficient for all the work to make it, and too much." In Hebrew that's dayam v'hoter: their enough, and more. Commentators have puzzled over it. How can something be exactly sufficient and also too much? The eighteenth-century commentator Or HaChaim offers a tender answer: there really was extra, but God made room for all of it in the work, so that no one who gave would see their gift set aside. There's a sharper note in the Jerusalem Talmud. It observes that this same people gave their gold for the calf, and gave their gold for the sanctuary. The generosity was the same both times. What changed was what it was for. And notice who says stop. Not the givers. The builders. It takes someone close to the work to see that the need is met, and the honesty to say so out loud, when it would be easy to keep taking.
screen: `MORNING AFTER MORNING, MORE.` · `THE BUILDERS SAY: ENOUGH.` · `DAYAM V'HOTER: ENOUGH, AND MORE.` · `THE SAME GOLD, A DIFFERENT AIM.` · then, large: `THEY HAD TO SAY STOP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice enough. Settle, and breathe. Look around wherever you are, slowly. The food in the kitchen. The clothes in the closet. The apps on the phone, the hours in the week, the people who love you. Pick one place where you already have enough, maybe more than enough, and simply say so to yourself: this is enough. Notice whether you believe it. Then breathe in, and breathe out, and let the wanting rest for a minute. The bell holds the time.
Vayakhel. The portion where Moses gathers the people, and they give so much that the builders have to ask them to stop.
Your line: they had to say stop. Today, when you reach for more of something, pause once and ask: is this already enough? Day three hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Jewish charity, tzedakah, is often given through communal funds, and the story of the overflowing gifts for the sanctuary is read each year in the portion Vayakhel.

original.note: Hebrew: their enough, and more, from Exodus 36:7.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice story about generous people.
what it means: the builders had the honesty to say the need was met, and the leader told everyone to stop giving.

what a scholar hears: 36:7 says both sufficient and too much (dayam v'hoter), a tension commentators have tried to resolve; Jerusalem Talmud Shekalim 1:1 sets the sanctuary gold beside the gold of the calf.
